title: Launch Day
paragraphs:
T minus ten minutes.
My new blazer is a spacesuit,
stiff at the shoulders, a size too big.
“You’ll grow into it,” says Mission Control,
straightening my tie for the third time
and pressing a packed lunch into my hands
like emergency supplies.

Three, two, one.
The front door seals behind me like an airlock,
and the bus blasts off
past the park, past the corner shop,
past my old school, where the little ones are lining up,
until everything I know
shrinks to a dot in the back window.

The new planet is enormous.
Its corridors twist like the inside of a shell,
the bell wails like a siren,
and giants in ties stride past me,
speaking a language I don’t understand:
periods, sets, double science.

At lunch, I float alone
in a galaxy of tables
where every seat is saved for someone else.
My tray is heavy. My mouth is dry.
Earth has never felt so far away.

Then a voice crackles through the silence:
“Are you lost too?”
A boy called Noah, his tie crooked,
his map held upside down.
We laugh. Then, two astronauts together,
we set off, charting every corridor and stair,
until the planet starts to shrink.

At four o’clock, I splash down at the kitchen table.
“How did it go?” asks Mission Control.
“Fine,” I say.
But what I mean is:
I landed.
I explored.
I can breathe here.

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 1.
Who do you think ‘Mission Control’ really is?
questions.model: Mission Control is the speaker’s mum or dad, who gets the speaker ready for the first day by straightening their tie and giving them a packed lunch.
points: a parent or carer, e.g. Mum or Dad. (Evidence might be that Mission Control straightens the speaker’s tie, packs their lunch and later asks ‘How did it go?’ at the kitchen table.)

questions.prompt:
Look at the whole poem.
What is the speaker really describing? Tick **one**.
options: a real journey into space
a dream about becoming an astronaut
a school trip to watch a rocket launch
their first day at a new school

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 3.
Find and copy **one** word that shows the corridors are not straight.

Look at verses 3 and 4.
How does the poet make the new school seem strange and frightening?
Give **two** examples from the poem and explain what each one suggests.
questions.model: The poet calls the school ‘The new planet’ and says it is ‘enormous’, which suggests that it feels huge and unfamiliar. The older pupils are ‘giants in ties’ who speak ‘a language I don’t understand’, which shows that the speaker feels small and confused by new words such as ‘periods, sets, double science’.
points: each example from verse 3 or 4 that is explained (1 mark each), such as:
‘The new planet is enormous’: the school feels huge and unfamiliar
the corridors ‘twist like the inside of a shell’: they are confusing and easy to get lost in
‘the bell wails like a siren’: the bell is loud and alarming
‘giants in ties’: the older pupils seem huge and scary
‘a language I don’t understand’: the new words (periods, sets, double science) are confusing
‘a galaxy of tables’: the dining hall is huge and the speaker feels tiny and alone
An example copied without an explanation does not score.

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 5.
Noah and the speaker set off, ‘charting every corridor and stair’.
Which word is closest in meaning to **charting**? Tick **one**.
options: cleaning
mapping
decorating
avoiding

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 5.
‘until the planet starts to shrink’
What does this suggest? Tick **one**.
options: The school is being knocked down.
The speaker is growing taller.
The school starts to feel smaller and less frightening as the speaker gets to know it.
The speaker and Noah get lost again.

questions.prompt:
Look at verse 6.
When Mission Control asks, ‘How did it go?’, what does the speaker reply?

Look at the whole poem.
Tick **one** box in each row to show whether each statement is **true** or **false**.
statements: The speaker’s blazer is a size too big.
The speaker travels to the new school by train.
Noah is holding his map upside down.
At lunch, the speaker sits with a big group of friends.

questions.prompt:
The poem begins with a countdown and ends with the speaker splashing down at home.
Why has the poet organised the poem like this? Tick **one**.
options: to show that the speaker is afraid of rockets
to show that the speaker’s school day was very short
to present the whole day as one space mission, from launch to landing
to show that the speaker would rather be an astronaut than go to school

questions.prompt:
How do the speaker’s feelings change during the day?
Explain, using evidence from the poem.
questions.model: At the start, the speaker feels nervous and small: the new school is ‘enormous’ and full of ‘giants in ties’ speaking ‘a language I don’t understand’. At lunch, the speaker feels lonely and homesick, floating ‘alone’ where ‘every seat is saved for someone else’, and ‘Earth has never felt so far away’. Meeting Noah changes things: they ‘laugh’ and explore together ‘until the planet starts to shrink’. By the end, the speaker feels relieved and proud. They only say ‘Fine’, but what they mean is ‘I landed’, ‘I explored’ and ‘I can breathe here’.
points: Describes how the speaker feels at the start or at lunch, such as nervous, lost or lonely, with evidence, such as ‘I float alone’ or ‘Earth has never felt so far away’.
Explains that meeting Noah makes the speaker feel better, with evidence, such as ‘We laugh’ or ‘until the planet starts to shrink’.
Explains how the speaker feels at the end, such as relieved, proud or at home, with evidence, such as ‘I landed’ or ‘I can breathe here’.

questions.prompt:
What do you think the speaker’s second day at the new school will be like?
Use evidence from the poem to support your prediction.
questions.model: I think the second day will be easier, because the speaker has made a friend, Noah, and they have already explored the school together, ‘charting every corridor and stair’. The school already seems smaller (‘the planet starts to shrink’), and the speaker says ‘I can breathe here’, so they will feel more relaxed.
points: a sensible prediction (1 mark), e.g. it will be easier or less frightening; the speaker will spend time with Noah; the speaker will not get lost.

evidence from the poem that supports the prediction (1 mark), e.g. the speaker has made a friend, Noah; they have explored ‘every corridor and stair’; ‘the planet starts to shrink’; ‘I can breathe here’.

questions.prompt: Which is the best summary of the whole poem? Tick **one**.
options: An astronaut is sent to a strange planet and never comes home.
A pupil misses the bus and arrives late on the first day at a new school.
A pupil describes their first day at a new school as if it were a space mission, from a lonely start to a hopeful end.
Two friends build a model rocket in a science lesson.
